blocks.text: A single host application rarely talks to just one MCP server. It usually talks to several at once, one for calendar, one for email, one for documents, one for search.
Each of those servers is its own little world. It answers the calls it gets and returns results, but it has no window into what the other servers were asked or what they said.
The host sits in the middle of all of it, and only the host can build a single unified picture of the conversation. This lesson is about how that picture gets built and shared.
1. One Host, Many Servers, One Model

blocks.alt: One Host, Many Servers, One Model
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803445-73025667.png
A typical MCP setup has one host application, one large language model, and any number of MCP servers connected to that host at the same time.
The model only ever sees one conversation. It does not know, or care, that a calendar answer and an email draft came from two completely different processes.

code.content:
# a host holding three live server connections at once
connected_servers = {
    "calendar": calendar_client,
    "email": email_client,
    "docs": docs_client,
}
# the model sees one conversation, built by the host from all three

blocks.text: 2. What Shared Context Actually Means
Shared context means a piece of information, or a decision, learned through one server is made available to the rest of the session, not locked inside that one exchange.
It could be a fact the calendar server returned, a choice the user made in response to a question, or a value the model decided on earlier in the same conversation.

blocks.title: Context here is not the model context window
blocks.content: This lesson uses context to mean a specific piece of retrieved information or a decision, not the whole token budget the model can hold. The two ideas are related, but they are not the same thing.

blocks.text: 3. Context Lives in the Host, Not in the Servers
An MCP server does not remember your other servers. It only remembers, if anything, its own calls within its own connection.
The host is the one piece of software present for every single call to every single server, which makes it the only natural place to keep a unified record.

items: A server knows only the requests sent directly to it
A server has no visibility into a sibling server it was never introduced to
The host is present across every server connection for the whole session
Only the host can compare, merge, or reuse information across servers

blocks.text: 4. A Concrete Example: Calendar Meets Email

blocks.alt: A Concrete Example: Calendar Meets Email
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803445-671470328.png
Say a user asks an assistant to reschedule a meeting and let the attendees know. The host calls the calendar server first, which returns a new meeting time.
Next the host calls the email server to send the update. If the host does not pass the new time along, the email server has absolutely no way of knowing what time was chosen.
The only reason the email server can write a correct message is that the host handed it the calendar result as part of its own request, not because the two servers spoke to each other.
5. The Risk: One Server Not Knowing What Another Told the LLM

blocks.alt: The Risk: One Server Not Knowing What Another Told the LLM
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803446-256409046.png
The central risk in a multi server session is simple to state. A server can be completely unaware of information the LLM already received from a different server in the same conversation.
If the host does not carry that information forward, the model may act on stale or partial facts, or worse, contradict something it already told the user a few turns earlier.
6. Why Servers Cannot Coordinate Directly
MCP servers are typically separate processes, sometimes on separate machines, started and stopped independently of each other by the host.
There is no protocol path for one server to reach out and ask another server what it just told the model, and there should not be, since that would break the isolation the architecture depends on.
Coordination, if it happens at all, has to be arranged by the host, which is the only party with a connection open to every server involved.
7. Building a Shared Context Object in the Host

blocks.alt: Building a Shared Context Object in the Host
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803446-952803862.png
7.1 A Simple Structure to Start With
The simplest fix is a plain object the host keeps in memory for the life of a session, holding facts and decisions as they are learned.
7.2 One Instance Per Session
The host creates one SharedContext per active conversation, not per server, so every server call in that session reads from and writes to the same object.
8. Updating Shared Context After Every Tool Call
The habit that makes this work is discipline. Every time a server returns something worth keeping, the host writes it into the shared object before moving on.

code.content:
meeting = await calendar_client.call_tool("reschedule_meeting", args)
shared_context.remember(
    key="meeting_time",
    value=meeting["new_time"],
    source="calendar_server",
)

blocks.text: Skipping this step for even one tool call is exactly how a gap opens up between what the model knows and what a later server call actually sends.
9. Passing Shared Context Into Every Server Interaction
Writing facts down is only half the job. The host also has to hand the relevant pieces back out whenever it builds the next request to any server.
That usually means folding relevant shared facts into the arguments of a tool call, or into the text the model sees before it decides what to do next.

blocks.title: Read before you build the request, not after
blocks.content: Pull the needed facts out of shared context while building the arguments for the next call, not as an afterthought once the call has already gone out with missing data.

blocks.text: 10. What Each Server Contributes vs What It Sees
It helps to lay out, server by server, what each one adds to shared context and what it actually needs handed back to it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Server","Contributes to shared context","Needs from shared context"],"rows":[["Calendar server","New meeting time, attendee list","Nothing from other servers, usually"],["Email server","Confirmation that a message was sent","Meeting time, attendee list"],["Docs server","Agenda document link","Meeting time, topic decided earlier"]]}

blocks.text: Notice the calendar server mostly contributes and rarely consumes, while the email and docs servers depend heavily on facts they never generated themselves.
11. Conflicting Information Across Servers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803447-805066286.png
Sometimes two servers report facts that do not agree, for example a calendar server and a separate scheduling server both claiming a meeting time, but different ones.
A host without a shared context object has no way to even notice the conflict, since each answer lives only in its own isolated exchange.

blocks.title: Newest is not always correct
blocks.content: When two servers disagree, simply trusting whichever answer arrived last can quietly propagate the wrong fact. A good host logs both values with their source and, where it matters, asks the user or re-checks before deciding which one to keep.

blocks.text: 12. Keeping a Single Source of Truth for Decisions
Decisions the user or the model made earlier deserve the same treatment as facts pulled from a server. Once a choice is made, it should be written down once and read from everywhere after that.
If the model re-decides the same thing twice, using slightly different reasoning each time, later servers can end up acting on two different versions of what was supposedly one decision.
13. Scoping: What Should and Should Not Be Shared

blocks.alt: Scoping: What Should and Should Not Be Shared
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803447-39427187.png
Not everything a server returns belongs in shared context. Sharing too much clutters the conversation and can leak information a server exposed for a narrow, internal reason.

items: Share facts that a later step could plausibly need, such as a chosen time, an id, or a decided value
Share decisions the user explicitly made, so they are not silently re-asked or re-decided
Avoid sharing raw, bulky server output that only one step ever needed
Avoid sharing sensitive details a server returned for its own internal use only

blocks.text: 14. Pattern: A Central Context Store
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803447-521109254.png
The pattern used throughout this lesson, one shared object the host reads and writes on every call, is the simplest version of what is sometimes called a central context store.
It works well for short and medium length sessions, and it keeps the mental model simple, one place to look for anything the session has learned so far.

code.content:
# the host keeps exactly one SharedContext for the whole session
session_context = SharedContext()
# every server client the host talks to is handed the same instance
calendar_client.attach_context(session_context)
email_client.attach_context(session_context)
docs_client.attach_context(session_context)

blocks.text: 15. Pattern: A Context Summary Per Turn
For longer sessions, a host can also build a short summary of shared context before each model turn, rather than handing over the entire raw history.
This keeps the unified view intact while trimming it down to what actually matters right now, which also helps with the token budget concerns covered elsewhere in this module.
Either pattern works. What matters is that the host, not any single server, owns the job of keeping that view coherent.
Worked Example
A travel assistant is connected to a flights server, a hotels server, and a calendar server. The user asks it to book a trip and block the dates.
The flights server returns a departure date. The host writes that date into shared context. The hotels server is then called with that same date, so it books a matching stay instead of guessing.

code.content:
flight = await flights_client.call_tool("book_flight", args)
shared_context.remember("trip_dates", flight["dates"], "flights_server")

hotel_args = {"dates": shared_context.get("trip_dates")}
await hotels_client.call_tool("book_hotel", hotel_args)

await calendar_client.call_tool(
    "block_dates",
    {"dates": shared_context.get("trip_dates")},
)

blocks.text: Every server after the first one worked off a date it never fetched itself. That only happened because the host carried it forward through one shared object.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a second server automatically knows what a first server already told the model
Forgetting to write a useful result into shared context right after the tool call that produced it
Sharing so much raw server output that the shared object becomes noisy and hard to trust
Trusting the most recently reported value during a conflict without checking its source
Re-asking the user for a decision that was already made earlier in the same session
Keeping shared context only in the model prompt and never in a structured object the host code can actually check

blocks.text: Practice
Design a SharedContext object for a host connected to a notes server, a search server, and a messaging server, then trace one conversation through it.

The user asks the assistant to find a document, summarize it, and message the summary to a colleague. Write out, step by step, what gets written into shared context after each server call, and what gets read back out before the next one.

code.content:
# fill in the calls and the remember and get steps for each one
doc = await search_client.call_tool("find_document", {"query": "Q3 plan"})
# TODO: remember the document id and title

summary = await notes_client.call_tool("summarize", {"doc_id": None})
# TODO: read the document id back out, then remember the summary

# TODO: read the summary back out and send it through the messaging client

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
A host talking to multiple MCP servers is the only place a unified view of the conversation can exist, because no server can see what another server told the model.
Keeping one shared context object, updated after every tool call and read before every new one, is what turns a set of isolated servers into a single coherent assistant.
